query: Which method can be used for phase stability, microstructure refinement, and property optimization, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Selective laser melting (SLM) processing of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloys refines the microstructure, enhances phase stability, and optimizes mechanical properties relative to conventional processing.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy produced via conventional annealing (with relatively coarse grains and lower dislocation density)
generation.intervention: Processing the alloy using SLM with controlled parameters (e.g., 90 W laser power, 600 mm/s scan speed, 25 µm layer thickness, using high‐purity argon environment and pre-alloyed spherical powder)
generation.conditions: Rapid solidification conditions inherent to SLM; controlled atmosphere; precise energy density (~75 J/mm³) and scanning pattern to promote uniform melting and solidification
generation.structural_mediator: A refined microstructure marked by nanometer-scale Mn₂O₃ precipitates at cell boundaries, high dislocation density, and directionally dependent grain sizes
generation.mechanism: Rapid solidification during SLM produces high thermal gradients that increase dislocation density and facilitate nanoprecipitate formation. These features contribute to Orowan strengthening and Zener drag effects that inhibit recrystallization and improve phase stability at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional processing, SLM-processed samples should exhibit a significantly higher yield strength (potentially near doubling at room temperature) and maintain superior mechanical properties up to ~700 °C, owing to the refined microstructure and nano-scale precipitates.
generation.baseline: Conventionally processed (annealed) HEA with lower dislocation density, coarser grains, and less pervasive nanoprecipitation resulting in lower yield strength and less stable high-temperature performance.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected up to temperatures where the nanoprecipitates and refined microstructure can effectively hinder dislocation motion (approximately ≤700 °C); behavior beyond this range remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvement in yield strength and high-temperature performance is not precisely established. Additionally, the influence of minor processing variations and the microstructural evolution at temperatures above 700 °C require further study.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy samples: one using conventional annealing and the other using SLM under the specified conditions. Characterize the microstructure using TEM (for grain size, dislocation density, and nanoprecipitate analysis) and evaluate mechanical properties via compression tests at room temperature and at temperatures up to 900 °C.
measurements: Size and distribution of Mn₂O₃ nanoprecipitates (via TEM/EDS)
Yield strength and stress–strain response at various temperatures (compression tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SLM processed samples do not display a significantly refined microstructure (i.e., substantially smaller grains, higher dislocation density, and evident nano-scale precipitates) and fail to show at least a 50% increase in yield strength at room temperature and comparable performance improvement at elevated temperatures (up to ~700 °C) relative to the conventionally processed samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: What are the temperature-dependent mechanical properties and deformation mechanisms of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy additively manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM) compared to conventionally processed alloys?. System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Selective laser melting (SLM) using pre-alloyed spherical powder (average diameter 27.2 µm); laser power 90 W, scan speed 600 mm/s, hatch space 80 µm, layer thickness 25 µm, volumetric energy density 75 J/mm³, 180° rotation scanning pattern, high-purity Ar atmosphere.. Test conditions: Compression tests at 25, 500, 600, 700, 800, and 900 °C; initial strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹; engineering strain limit 0.4; specimens preheated at 10 °C/min; MoS₂ lubricant used..
